chapters.title: Chapter 2: Behavioral Economics in Everyday Money Decisions

lessons.title: Default Options: Why EPF and NPS Auto-Enrolment Changes Behavior

children.text: The day Vikram joined his first job in Bengaluru, HR handed him a form. His Employees' Provident Fund contribution was set at 12% of basic pay, matched by his employer, with a box further down for Voluntary Provident Fund if he wanted to save more at the same assured, tax-advantaged rate. He signed where marked and never opened that form again. Thirty years and several appraisals later, his contribution rate is exactly what it was on day one. He never actively chose 12%. He never actively chose against the voluntary top-up either. Both were decided the moment he signed a form he barely read, by whoever designed the form. This is the default effect, and it is the single most powerful nudge in this entire course.

body.text: When one option is pre-set as what happens if a person does nothing, an overwhelming majority of people end up with that option, regardless of whether it actually suits them. The default is not just one choice among many. For most people, it is the only choice that actually gets made.

children.text: The Default Effect: Doing Nothing Is Still a Choice

markDefs.definition: The tendency for people to stick overwhelmingly with whatever option is pre-set to happen automatically if they take no action, even when switching away requires very little effort.

The broader tendency to prefer things stay as they currently are, even after having actively chosen the current state in the past. Related to the default effect but not identical: status quo bias can exist even when nobody set an external default.

children.text: The
default effect
is a close cousin of the broader
status quo bias

you met in Chapter 1, where Rohan never switched out of his employer's default pension fund in eight years. The two overlap but are not identical: status quo bias is a general reluctance to change anything about your current situation. The default effect is more specific, it is what happens the moment someone else pre-sets an option for you. Three forces make defaults unusually sticky:
Implied endorsement.
People assume whoever set the default, an employer, a regulator, an app, knew what they were doing, so the default reads as the sensible, recommended option.
Effort, however small.
Switching requires finding the right form or setting, reading it, and acting, and that small effort is often enough to be skipped indefinitely in a busy life.
Loss framing.

Moving away from a default feels like giving something up, even when it is simply choosing a different, equally available option, because loss aversion makes any change from the reference point feel risky.
The Classic Evidence: Two Studies That Made Defaults Famous

body.caption: Two landmark studies on the power of a default

cells: A US company switched its retirement plan from opt-in enrolment to automatic enrolment with an opt-out
Participation rose from roughly 37% to roughly 86% among new employees, with no change to the plan itself
Compared organ donor consent rates between opt-in countries and opt-out countries
Opt-out countries recorded consent rates often above 90%, versus well under 20% in similar opt-in countries, from the default alone

body.text: In both studies, the actual decision available to people never changed. Anyone could opt out of the retirement plan or the organ donor registry, and anyone could opt in. The only thing that moved was which box was already ticked. That single design choice outweighed years of financial-literacy campaigns and public health messaging combined.

children.text: Defaults in Indian Retirement Savings: EPF, VPF, and NPS

India runs the same mechanism at national scale, in two different retirement systems. Under the EPF Act, an eligible employee's 12% contribution rate, matched by the employer, is set the day they join and almost never revisited. Voluntary Provident Fund lets any EPF member contribute more from their own salary at the same assured, government-notified interest rate, through a single form change with their employer's payroll or HR team. It requires no new account, no new paperwork beyond that form, and offers a materially higher, tax-advantaged, guaranteed return than most bank fixed deposits. Very few employees ever use it, not because it is a bad option, but because it is not the default one.

markDefs.definition: The pre-set NPS investment option for any subscriber who does not actively pick their own equity, corporate bond, and government securities mix. Its default variant, LC-50, allocates up to 50% to equity for younger subscribers and automatically reduces equity exposure as they age.

children.text: The National Pension System shows the same pattern from a different angle. Every NPS subscriber can pick their own mix of equity, corporate debt, and government securities under "Active Choice." Anyone who does not actively pick is placed into
Auto Choice

, a lifecycle fund that automatically shifts a subscriber's allocation from more equity in their twenties and thirties toward more debt as they approach retirement, without the subscriber lifting a finger. This default is genuinely well designed, built around a sensible age-based glide path rather than a careless one. But most NPS subscribers, including plenty who could benefit from actively customising their mix given their own risk appetite and other investments, simply never touch the setting, for exactly the same three reasons any default sticks.

body.title: Which force is at work?
body.question: An NPS subscriber says, "I figured PFRDA designed Auto Choice for a reason, so switching to Active Choice felt like second-guessing an expert." Which of the three forces behind default stickiness does this best illustrate?
body.explanation: The subscriber is treating the default as a signal of expert judgment rather than simply the option requiring the least action, which is implied endorsement. Effort would show up as "I never got around to it," and loss framing would show up as "switching felt like giving something up."

children.text: When Defaults Work For You, and When They Work Against You

A default is not automatically good just because it uses the same mechanism as a bad one. The mandatory 12% EPF default forces long-term saving most people would under-save without it, a form of paternalism most economists consider justified, given how consistently people underestimate their own retirement needs. The same mechanism, aimed the other way, is the sludge you met in Chapter 1: an auto-renewing subscription, a pre-ticked insurance add-on at checkout, a food delivery app defaulting to the priciest delivery slot. The design is identical. Only who benefits from the inertia changes.

cells: The employee's own long-term financial security
Yes, stated plainly on every payslip
Often buried in fine print at sign-up
Reasonably, through a standard HR or EPFO process
Frequently made deliberately difficult, the sludge pattern from Chapter 1

body.title: Is this default paternalism or sludge?
body.scenario: A new mutual fund SIP platform automatically enrols every new investor into a small "step-up" feature that increases their monthly SIP amount by 10% every year, clearly disclosed at sign-up in the same font size as the rest of the form, with a one-tap toggle to turn it off at any time from the account settings.
body.prompt: Using the criteria from the table above, is this closer to a good default or to sludge, and why?
body.modelAnswer:
1. It is closer to a good default. The inertia benefits the investor directly, since a step-up SIP that keeps pace with rising income is a well-documented way to counter under-saving over time.
2. It passes the disclosure test: the feature is stated clearly at sign-up, not hidden in fine print, which is the opposite of the confirm-shaming and interface-interference patterns covered in Chapter 1.
3. It passes the ease-of-exit test: a one-tap toggle available any time is genuinely low friction, unlike a subscription that requires a phone call to cancel.
4. The one thing worth watching is whether the 10% step-up rate itself was chosen to suit typical investors' income growth, or simply set high enough to maximise assets under management for the platform. A well-designed default should be defensible on the user's behalf, not just technically compliant with disclosure rules.

body.title: Name the mechanism
body.textWithBlank: The tendency for people to overwhelmingly stick with whatever option is pre-set to happen if they take no action is called the ___ effect.
body.explanation: The default effect is specifically about a pre-set option, distinct from the broader status quo bias, which can apply even when no one has externally set a default at all.

body.title: A cousin nudge: automatically escalating your own savings rate

children.text: In 2004, Richard Thaler and Shlomi Benartzi published "Save More Tomorrow," a program that let employees commit in advance to putting a portion of each future pay raise into their retirement account automatically, rather than asking them to cut their current take-home pay right away. Because the increase only ever applied to money they had not yet received, it sidestepped loss aversion almost entirely. In the original study, participants' contribution rates rose from roughly 3.5% to roughly 13.6% of salary over a series of pay raises, almost entirely through default design rather than persuasion. The mutual fund step-up SIP in the scenario above is a direct descendant of this idea.

body.label: How much a default alone can move behavior
body.context: Madrian and Shea's 2001 study found automatic enrolment alone lifted US retirement plan participation this much, with the plan itself completely unchanged.

cards.definition: The tendency for people to stick overwhelmingly with a pre-set option that applies automatically if they take no action.
The broader tendency to prefer the current state of affairs, related to but distinct from the default effect, since it can apply even without an externally set default.
The assumption that a pre-set default must be the sensible or recommended option, simply because someone in authority set it.
The default NPS investment option, a lifecycle fund that automatically shifts a subscriber's equity-to-debt mix as they age, used by anyone who does not actively select their own allocation.
A default designed to benefit whoever set it rather than the person defaulted into it, such as an auto-renewing subscription with deliberately difficult cancellation.

points: The default effect means the pre-set option, not the objectively best option, is what most people actually end up with, driven by implied endorsement, switching effort, and loss framing.
Landmark studies on retirement plans and organ donation both found defaults alone moved behavior far more than persuasion or education campaigns did, without changing the underlying choice at all.

EPF's mandatory 12% default and NPS's Auto Choice lifecycle fund are large-scale, real Indian examples, while Voluntary Provident Fund shows how a genuinely good, low-effort option can go almost unused simply for not being the default.

The same default mechanism can serve the user, as in EPF auto-enrolment, or work against them, as in sludge-style auto-renewals, and the test is who benefits from the inertia and how easy the exit genuinely is.
Automatic escalation programs like Save More Tomorrow show how default design can be used deliberately for a person's own long-term benefit, by applying the default only to money not yet in hand.
